label: Euclidean Geometry Inside the Projective Plane
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 329 through 348. The big idea is that Euclidean geometry is not separate from projective geometry; it is projective geometry plus one distinguished pair of complex points on the line at infinity. Fixing that pair lets a purely projective plane remember circles, angles, and right angles.

label: The Two Circular Points I and J
notes: Introduce the absolute points. They live on the line at infinity, they are complex conjugates, and they satisfy the imaginary relation that makes every circle vanish on them. Stress that they are anchors, never sampled real points, so students do not look for them on a drawn circle.

label: Every Circle Passes Through I and J
notes: Show the substitution explicitly. A general circle in homogeneous coordinates has the same leading quadratic part, and feeding in either circular point kills the equation because the imaginary unit squares to minus one. This is why all circles share the two absolute points and form a pencil-like family through them.

label: Circles Are Conics Through I and J
notes: Reframe a circle as a conic constrained to pass through the absolute pair. A conic has five degrees of freedom; forcing it through I and J consumes two, leaving three, exactly the centre and radius of a circle. This is the key dictionary entry connecting projective conics to Euclidean circles.

label: Cocircularity Is a Six-Point Conic Test
notes: Translate the Euclidean notion that four points lie on a circle into the projective statement that those four points together with I and J lie on one conic. Present the bracket identity as the computable certificate, and emphasize that a drawing is suggestive but the bracket residual is the actual proof.

label: Perpendicularity Is Harmonic Conjugacy
notes: Two finite lines hit the line at infinity in two ideal direction points. The lines are perpendicular exactly when that pair is harmonic with respect to I and J, giving cross-ratio minus one. Make clear this is the right-angle special case of the general angle formula that follows.

label: Laguerre's Formula for Angle
notes: State Laguerre's formula: the angle between two lines is one over two i times the logarithm of the cross-ratio of their ideal directions with the circular points. Explain the half and the i convert a multiplicative cross-ratio into an additive real angle, and why measurement is modulo pi for unoriented lines.

label: Reading the Angle as a Cross-Ratio
notes: Walk through the construction geometrically. From the intersection of the two lines, draw the four lines to L, M, I, and J; the cross-ratio of that pencil encodes the angle. Connect the harmonic right-angle case to the general logarithmic case so students see one formula specializing to the other.

label: Similarities Preserve the Pair {I,J}
notes: Characterize Euclidean transformations projectively. Orientation-preserving similarities fix each circular point; reflections swap them; either way the unordered pair is preserved. A shear keeps the line at infinity but moves I and J, which is exactly why it is affine but not a similarity.

label: The Transformation Hierarchy
notes: Lay out the nested hierarchy from projective down to Euclidean motions, keyed by what each level preserves. Projective keeps cross-ratio, affine keeps the line at infinity, similarity keeps the pair I and J, and isometry adds an absolute unit. This makes the taxonomy concrete rather than just a list.

label: Distance Needs a Reference Segment
notes: Explain why distance is the one Euclidean quantity the circular pair alone cannot recover, since similarities rescale. Introduce a unit reference segment, then present the bracket distance formula. With the unit fixed, even absolute length is written entirely in projective brackets through I and J.

label: What Survives Which Transformation
notes: Close with the diagnostic lab. Track a circle, an angle, and a segment under a motion, a scaling similarity, and a shear, and watch which invariants survive. The hierarchy from earlier appears in numbers, reinforcing that the circular points are the projective memory of Euclidean structure.

label: Recap: The Projective Memory of Euclid
notes: Summarize the chapter as a single move: mark I and J, and Euclidean geometry reappears inside the projective plane. Circles, angles, perpendicularity, and similarities all become statements about the absolute pair, and distance follows once a unit segment is chosen.
